exam-05-q01.why_correct_en:
Easter falls in March or April because it is a movable Christian festival. In Western churches, Easter Sunday is the first Sunday after the first full moon following the spring equinox, so its calendar date changes each year.

Common UK customs include Easter Sunday church services, chocolate Easter eggs, Easter Bunny stories and egg hunts. Eggs represent new life and are sometimes linked to the stone at Jesus's tomb. Hot cross buns are traditionally associated with Good Friday; decorated eggs, egg rolling and Easter bonnets also survive in some communities.

exam-05-q02.why_correct_en: 25p is not a normal UK coin denomination. Current circulating coins are 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2; the heptagonal 20p and 50p coins can help prevent confusion with the invented 25p option.

exam-05-q03.why_correct_en: The Eden Project is in Cornwall, near St Austell. Its enormous geodesic Biomes were built in a former china-clay pit and contain plants from rainforest and Mediterranean climates, turning an industrial landscape into an environmental visitor attraction.

exam-05-q04.why_correct_en: False. St Helena and the Falkland Islands are British Overseas Territories, not constituent parts of Great Britain or the United Kingdom. The UK is responsible for matters such as defence and foreign affairs, while each territory has its own local constitutional arrangements.

exam-05-q05.why_correct_en: The rule of law and democracy are two fundamental principles of British life. The full set also includes individual liberty, mutual respect and tolerance of different faiths and beliefs, and participation in community life.

exam-05-q06.why_correct_en: Potential jurors are selected using the electoral register, so eligible people need to be registered to vote. Selection is random and registration does not guarantee service; courts then apply the relevant age, residence and disqualification rules.

exam-05-q07.why_correct_en: The Church of Scotland is Presbyterian. It is governed through councils of ministers and elders rather than bishops, and although it is Scotland's national church it is constitutionally independent of the state.

exam-05-q08.why_correct_en:
Modern golf developed in Scotland, but it was not invented by one known person on a single date. It evolved from medieval stick-and-ball games. Players first used streets and churchyards; Scotland's coastal links provided firm, well-drained turf and natural hollows that became hazards, making them ideal places to play a ball through a series of holes.

Scotland's earliest surviving written reference is James II's 1457 ban, issued because golf distracted men from compulsory archery practice. Royal and noble participation later helped move the game onto designated grounds with specialist clubs. The Company of Gentlemen Golfers wrote the earliest surviving 13 rules in Edinburgh in 1744. Early courses had different numbers of holes; the influence of St Andrews and The R&A helped make 18 holes the accepted standard by the late nineteenth century.

exam-05-q09.why_correct_en: April Fool's Day is on 1 April, when newspapers and broadcasters traditionally publish convincing joke stories until midday. The prank is often revealed later, training readers to notice improbable details and check sources.

exam-05-q10.why_correct_en: Charles II is the correct answer. After the Royalist defeat at Worcester in 1651, he hid in an oak tree at Boscobel House while escaping Parliament's forces, eventually reaching France. The episode is remembered in many places and pubs named the Royal Oak.

exam-05-q11.why_correct_en: Henry VIII was Elizabeth I's father; her mother was Anne Boleyn. Elizabeth was declared illegitimate after Anne's execution but later restored to the succession, becoming queen in 1558 and ruling for 44 years.

exam-05-q12.why_correct_en: False. A police complaint is not limited to a written letter to one commissioner. It may be made directly to the police force or through the independent oversight body for the relevant UK nation; the bodies and procedures differ across England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

exam-05-q13.why_correct_en:
St Patrick is the patron saint associated with Northern Ireland and Ireland. St Patrick's Day is 17 March, traditionally his death date.

A shamrock is a small clover-like plant with three leaflets at the end of one stalk. The Christian Trinity means that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three distinct persons but one God. A later tradition says that St Patrick held up a shamrock and used its three leaflets on one plant as a simple comparison. This is why the shamrock became closely associated with St Patrick's Day and Ireland, although there is no direct record of the story from Patrick's lifetime.

exam-05-q14.why_correct_en: The Enlightenment was the 17th- and 18th-century movement that emphasised reason, observation and debate about science, government and individual rights. British figures included John Locke, David Hume and Adam Smith, whose ideas influenced modern democracy and economics.

exam-05-q15.why_correct_en:
Mary, Queen of Scots was Catholic, while her cousin Elizabeth I was Protestant. Mary's religion and claim to the English throne made her a focus for Catholic plots; after years in English custody, she was executed in 1587.

Catholics and Protestants are both Christians who affirm Jesus Christ, the Bible and the Trinity. The Catholic Church is a worldwide communion led by the Pope and bishops; it receives doctrine through Scripture and Apostolic Tradition, interpreted by the Church's teaching authority, and recognises seven sacraments. Protestant is an umbrella term for many traditions that emerged from the sixteenth-century Reformation. They reject the Pope's universal jurisdiction, place greater emphasis on Scripture as the highest norm and on salvation by God's grace through faith. Many recognise Baptism and Holy Communion as the two principal Gospel sacraments, but Anglican, Presbyterian and other Protestant churches differ considerably in worship and government.

exam-05-q16.why_correct_en: Workplace discrimination is generally a civil-law matter: an individual may bring a claim in an employment tribunal and seek a remedy such as compensation. This differs from a criminal prosecution brought by the state, although some conduct can involve both civil and criminal law.

exam-05-q17.why_correct_en: Admiral Nelson died at the Battle of Trafalgar on 21 October 1805. His fleet defeated the combined French and Spanish fleets, preventing Napoleon from gaining control of the sea; Nelson was shot aboard HMS Victory and died after learning that victory was secure.

exam-05-q18.why_correct_en: The event is called the Glorious Revolution of 1688. William of Orange landed with an army, James II lost political and military support and fled, and William III and Mary II accepted the crown subject to the 1689 Bill of Rights, strengthening Parliament's constitutional position.

exam-05-q19.why_correct_en: Friends of the Earth is an environmental charity and campaigning network. It works on issues such as climate change, pollution and protection of nature, using local groups, public campaigns and legal or policy advocacy.

exam-05-q20.why_correct_en: True. Marriage does not create permanent consent to sex. A husband who intentionally penetrates his wife without her consent, and without reasonably believing that she consents, can be prosecuted for rape; English law definitively rejected the old marital-rape exemption in 1991.

exam-05-q21.why_correct_en: The Boer War of 1899–1902 was fought in South Africa between the British Empire and the two Boer republics, the South African Republic and Orange Free State. The Boers were largely descendants of Dutch-speaking settlers, and the conflict ended with British victory and later political union.

exam-05-q22.why_correct_en: Canvassing means contacting voters to persuade them to support a party or candidate, commonly by knocking on doors, telephoning or speaking in public places. Campaigners also record issues raised by voters and encourage supporters to vote on polling day.

exam-05-q23.why_correct_en: The Lord of the Rings by J. R. R. Tolkien won the BBC's 2003 Big Read poll as the nation's best-loved novel. Tolkien was an Oxford philologist, and his knowledge of Old and Middle English helped shape the languages, names and mythology of Middle-earth.

exam-05-q24.why_correct_en: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September after their demand for withdrawal was ignored, marking the beginning of the Second World War in Europe.
